reply: It's been three days with a dry, hacking cough. I've been burning up, on and off, and didn't have a thermometer, but I was definitely roasting. Since yesterday I've been bringing up stuff—rusty, brownish stuff at first, then clear. There's a sharp pain on the right side, near my back, that catches when I breathe deep or cough. utterance: That sounds miserable. A few important questions to help work out what's causing this. Are you short of breath—either at rest or when you move around? Have you had shaking chills or rigors? Any blood in what you cough up, beyond that rusty colour? And any other symptoms—headache, sore throat, runny nose, muscle aches, or an upset stomach?
reply: I got puffed going up the stairs and on the way in from the car park, but I'm alright sitting here. The first night I was shaking under the doona, teeth chattering, even though I was boiling. I haven't had any actual blood, just that rusty colour. I don't know what rigors mean—can you explain?

utterance:
Good question — a "rigor" is exactly what you described: an episode of uncontrollable shaking and chattering teeth even though you feel burning hot. It usually comes with a spike in fever, and it often points to a bacterial infection rather than a simple cold.

Now some background questions. Do you have any medical conditions—asthma, diabetes, heart or lung problems? Do you smoke or vape, now or in the past? How much alcohol do you drink in a typical week? Are you on any regular medications, and do you have any allergies to medicines? Have you had a flu or COVID vaccine this year? And has anyone around you—at school or at home—been sick lately?
reply: That's a lot at once. I'm not sure where to start. What would you like to know first?

utterance: Fair enough — one at a time. First: do you have any ongoing medical conditions, like asthma, diabetes, or heart or lung problems?
reply: No, I don't have asthma or anything with my lungs, no diabetes, and no heart problems.

utterance: That's really important to know — thank you. A reaction with hives and swollen lips to penicillin means I must avoid penicillin-type antibiotics for you. Which blood pressure medication are you taking?

utterance:
Here's what's going on, Mark. You have pneumonia — an infection in the lower part of your right lung. It explains everything: the fever with that shaking chill, the rusty-coloured phlegm, and the sharp pain when you breathe in deeply, which is the inflamed lung rubbing against its lining.

The good news: you're otherwise healthy, your oxygen level is reasonable, and your observations are stable, so you're safe to be treated at home with tablets rather than in hospital.

You do need an antibiotic — but because of your penicillin reaction as a child, I've prescribed doxycycline instead, one 100 mg tablet once a day for five days. Take it with food and a full glass of water, and don't lie down for half an hour after it, as it can irritate the gullet. It can also make your skin burn more easily in the sun, so be sun-smart this week. I've also given you paracetamol — two 500 mg tablets up to four times a day for the fever and aches.

For the next few days: rest, plenty of fluids, and stay home from school until the fever has settled — you're contagious and you'll recover faster if you rest. I'd like to see you again in two to three days to make sure you're turning the corner.

Now the important part — when to get urgent help. Come back immediately, or call triple zero, if you become much more breathless at rest, the chest pain becomes severe, you cough up blood, you feel confused or drowsy, or you're vomiting and can't keep fluids or the tablets down. And if you're not clearly improving within two to three days, I want to see you sooner rather than later.

Any questions about any of that?
reply: No questions, doc. Just... thanks. I'll take the pills and rest. I'll stay home from school. I hope I'm not making things worse by being sick.

utterance:
You're doing exactly the right thing — catching this early and resting is what gets you better fastest. You couldn't have prevented it, so no guilt there. Most people with your picture are much improved within a week, though the tiredness and cough can linger for a few weeks.

When I see you in a couple of days, if things aren't fully settling we may organise a chest X-ray to double-check everything's clearing. And when you're well again, let's talk about a flu shot before next winter — it won't stop everything, but it lowers your chances of ending up back here like this.

Take care, Mark. See you in two to three days — sooner if any of those warning signs appear.
reply: I'm not going downhill fast. It's worse than the first day, but about the same since yesterday.
